title: Stripe-based activation redistributor: proposal and notes
body:
Purpose

This note sketches a lightweight, incrementally deployable design for redistributing intermediate activations across multiple GPUs at serving time to reduce NCCL hot-spots and improve utilization in heterogeneous NVLink topologies. I’m calling the core idea "stripe-based activation redistribution": split activation tensors into narrow stripes and map stripes to NVLink-connected peers so collective traffic is spread across links and compute.

Motivation / Problem statement

Observed behavior in multi-GPU inference: when we run tensor-parallel (TP) or pipeline-parallel (PP) configurations the communication workload often concentrates on a small set of links or ranks (e.g., the rank owning the largest shard of an attention head), causing:
- microbursting on NCCL/ring channels leading to latency tail spikes
- under-utilization of GPUs with spare compute (imbalanced kernel mapping)
- cache thrash for KV caches when a single rank becomes the primary source for many requests

Existing mitigations (layer re-ordering, static sharding, NCCL tuning knobs) help but are brittle in heterogenous fleets and under dynamic workloads (mixed sequence lengths, variable batch shapes). We need a run-time mechanism that:
- spreads activation traffic across multiple physical interconnects (NVLink islands, PCIe paths)
- is scheduler-friendly and incremental (doesn’t require full model rewrites)
- interacts sanely with KV cache (no accidental cache invalidations)

High-level idea

1) On a per-layer (or per-attention-block) basis, split activation tensors along a contiguous dimension into N stripes (small contiguous shards). Usually split along sequence-length or feature dim depending on kernel semantics.
2) Dynamically map each stripe to a different serving rank/GPU in the same allocation, selected to maximize NVLink locality (prefer NVLink/IB neighbors), but deliberately spread so heavy collectives touch multiple links.
3) Locally execute the kernel for each stripe on its assigned GPU; for kernels that require full-reduction (e.g., softmax across heads), perform a staged combine across stripe owners using neighborhood collectives to avoid single-hop concentration.
4) Merge stripe outputs (stitch) before the next layer or before returning outputs to the client. Stripe boundaries are metadata-only for most kernels; stitching is a low-cost concat in most runtimes.

Why this helps

- By splitting tensors and mapping stripes to different physical links, NCCL collective traffic is parallelized across multiple channels instead of all flows funneling through one link.
- Smaller per-stripe kernel invocations improve compute/communication overlap and allow microbatching strategies that reduce tail latency for short sequences.
- The approach is elastic: stripe count can be tuned based on sequence length, model size, and topology.

Design details

Stripe sizing heuristics
- default stripe width = max(1, floor(feature_dim / 4)) for attention ops (tuneable).
- For very short sequences (<= 8) avoid striping across seq-dim; prefer feature-dim or skip striping.
- Cap maximum stripes per layer to avoid explosion of small kernels (default 8).
- Auto-adjust stripes based on recent latency/cost telemetry (feedback loop in Optimize).

Topology-aware mapper
- Input: allocation topology (list of GPUs, NVLink adjacency matrix, PCIe group ids), current model kernel type, stripe count.
- Greedy selection: pick first stripe owner = layer's canonical owner (to preserve cache locality), then choose subsequent owners by highest NVLink bandwidth to canonical owner but preferring different physical links.
- Fallback: if NVLink adjacency is poor, prefer same host (PCIe local) then remote.

KV cache interaction
- Keep KV cache keys sharded using a deterministic stripe-affinity mapping so that reading/writing KV entries is colocated with stripe compute when possible.
- When stripe owners differ across layers, cache reads may need scatter/gather. Mitigation: keep a small per-rank prefix cache replication for hot prefixes (configurable).
- On cache warmup, prefer canonical owner for writes; enable background prefix sync to stripe owners to reduce on-path scatter.

Kernel mapping and micro-kernels
- Two paths: (A) Native kernel support for partial-stripe inputs (preferred), (B) Host/driver slicing and invoking existing kernels per-stripe (fallback).
- Prefer kernels that accept contiguous memory regions to avoid extra copies; where unavoidable, perform zero-copy view creation.
- For ops with expensive global reductions (layernorm across features), perform a two-stage algorithm: local partial reduce on stripes, cross-stripe reduce via neighborhood allreduce with limited fan-in.

NCCL tuning and neighborhood collectives
- Avoid global allreduce across all stripe owners when possible. Use hierarchical/neighborhood collectives:
  - local NVLink allreduce within a host or NVLink island
  - inter-host ribbon/IB collective for aggregated partials
- Leverage NCCL group APIs to coalesce launches across stripes so NCCL can schedule efficient collectives.
- Tune NCCL launch priorities and buffer sizes for stripe-sized transfers (smaller buffers favor latency).

Failure modes and fallbacks
- If stripe owner becomes unavailable or overloaded, runtime switches to canonical single-owner mode for that layer (atomic fallback).
- If KV cache misses with high scatter overhead, reduce stripe count for affected route until cache stabilizes.

Measurements / success criteria
- Primary metrics: 99th percentile token-latency reduction, average GPU link utilization, reduction in NCCL retransmits/timeout events, overall throughput for common workloads.
- Secondary: increase in per-request memory copies, additional scheduling overhead (ms).

Planned experiments (short-term)
1) Microbench: implement driver-level stripe slicing + existing kernels. Run A-B against baseline on 8xA100 host with mixed seq-lengths. Measure latency distribution and PCIe/NVLink utilization.
2) Topology probe: gather adjacency matrices for our most common instance types, validate mapper heuristics.
3) KV-coupled run: simulate cached and cold-cache scenarios with stripe mapping and measure extra scatter/gather costs.
4) NCCL tuning sweep: buffer-size, group-size, and collective hierarchy patterns.

Pseudo-code: stripe mapper (sketch)

function choose_stripe_owners(allocation, layer_owner, stripe_count, adjacency):
  owners = [layer_owner]
  candidates = allocation.gpu_list - {layer_owner}
  while owners.length < stripe_count and candidates not empty:
    pick = argmax(candidates, lambda g: adjacency.bandwidth(layer_owner, g) * novelty_score(g, owners))
    owners.append(pick)
    candidates.remove(pick)
  return owners

Operational rollout plan
- Phase 1 (internal): driver slicing + standard kernels, feature-flagged per-route. Only enabled for experimental fleet.
- Phase 2 (optimized kernels): add stripe-aware kernels for attention/qk/gemm critical path. Expand to staging.
- Phase 3 (gradual rollout): enable automatic stripe count tuning and telemetry-driven rollout to more customers.

Open questions / risks
- How much extra copy overhead will striping introduce in practice for long sequences? (measure)
- Interaction with quantized kernels and tensor layouts (NHWC vs NCHW-like shapes) — will require kernel work.
- Memory fragmentation risk if many small stripes allocated concurrently.
- Security / cross-tenant considerations for Dedicated/Private deployments — need to ensure no data leakage when stripes map across different security domains (probably disallow across tenant boundaries).

Action items
- Diego: prototype host-level stripe slicing + driver invocation (2 weeks).
- Liang: collect topology data from production fleets and build adjacency service (1 week).
- Samantha: write microbench harness comparing stripe counts on 8xA100 and 4xH100 (2 weeks).
- Marcus: design KV prefix replication policy and draft config knobs for cache replication (1 week).

Notes / fringe ideas
- Adaptive stripe sizing per-request using a cheap estimator (based on seq-length and recent per-route latency history).
- Use striping only for heavy layers (self-attention projection) and keep small feed-forward layers unstriped to limit overhead.
- For pipeline parallel setups, stripe across stages to balance both intra-stage and inter-stage communication.

If this approach looks promising I will open an RFC PR in the runtime repo with an initial driver-prototype plan and some microbench results from Diego. For now marking as draft.

References
- internal runbook: CONFLUENCE-RT/stripe-activation-arch (link above)
- similar ideas in literature: hierarchical allreduce papers, NCCL neighborhood collectives notes
